title: 3-Read Friday #98: Atomisation, Teacher Humor, and Misused Education Terms
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #98 opens with Kris Boulton correcting a widespread misreading of his own Atomisation framework: Atomisation is not the same as breaking mathematics into small procedural steps, but the decomposition of cognitive routines into conceptual atoms that expose deep mathematical structure and relationships between ideas. Andrew Watson then reviews research on teacher humour, finding that on-topic humour modestly improves students' perceptions of teachers and lessons while aggressive humour actively harms them. Michael Rose closes the issue with a critical, half-satirical survey of 26 terms modern education repeatedly misuses. Barton frames the Boulton piece as important enough to revisit on his podcast, signalling that the terminology confusion around Atomisation is a live and consequential debate in the maths-education community.
points: Atomisation, properly understood, is about decomposing cognitive routines into conceptual atoms that reveal mathematical structure -- not simply chunking procedures into smaller steps, a distinction Boulton considers a common and consequential misreading.
Watson's research review draws a clean line between two kinds of classroom humour: on-topic humour modestly helps perceptions of teaching, while aggressive humour reliably hurts them.
Rose's list of misused education terms functions as a check on jargon drift -- worth using as a discussion prompt for how carelessly language gets adopted in the field.
Barton signals the Boulton correction is significant enough to warrant a dedicated podcast follow-up, not just a newsletter mention.
